verses.zh: （以斯拉人以探的训诲诗。）我要歌唱耶和华的慈爱，直到永远；我要用口将你的信实传与万代。
verses.en: A well-written song[NOTE:1] by Ethan the Ezrahite.I will sing continually[NOTE:2] about the Lord’s faithful deeds;to future generations I will proclaim your faithfulness.[NOTE:3]
notes: Psalm 89. The psalmist praises God as the sovereign creator of the world. He recalls God’s covenant with David, but then laments that the promises of the covenant remain unrealized. The covenant promised the Davidic king military victories, but the king has now been subjected to humiliating defeat.
The meaning of the Hebrew term מַשְׂכִּיל (maskil) is uncertain. See the note on the phrase “well-written song” in the superscription of Ps 88.
Or “forever.”

verses.zh: 因我曾说：你的慈悲必建立到永远；你的信实必坚立在天上。
verses.en: For I say, “Loyal love is permanently established;[NOTE:1] in the skies you set up your faithfulness.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “to a generation and a generation I will make known your faithfulness with my mouth.”
Heb “built.”

verses.zh: 我与我所拣选的人立了约，向我的仆人大卫起了誓：
verses.en: The Lord said,[NOTE:1] “I have made a covenant with my chosen one;I have made a promise on oath to David, my servant:
notes: You set up your faithfulness. This may allude to the Lord’s heavenly throne, which symbolizes his just rule and from which the Lord decrees his unconditional promises (see vv. 8, 14).

verses.zh: 我要建立你的后裔，直到永远；要建立你的宝座，直到万代。（细拉）
verses.en: ‘I will give you an eternal dynasty[NOTE:1] and establish your throne throughout future generations.’”[NOTE:2] (Selah)
notes: The words “the Lord said” are supplied in the translation for clarification. It is clear that the words of vv. 3-4 are spoken by the Lord, in contrast to vv. 1-2, which are spoken by the psalmist.
Heb “forever I will establish your offspring.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，诸天要称赞你的奇事；在圣者的会中，要称赞你的信实。
verses.en: O Lord, the heavens[NOTE:1] praise your amazing deeds,as well as your faithfulness in the angelic assembly.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and I will build to a generation and a generation your throne.”
As the following context makes clear, the personified “heavens” here stand by metonymy for the angelic beings that surround God’s heavenly throne.

verses.zh: 在天空谁能比耶和华呢？　神的众子中，谁能像耶和华呢？
verses.en: For who in the skies can compare to the Lord?Who is like the Lord among the heavenly beings,[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “in the assembly of the holy ones.” The phrase “holy ones” sometimes refers to God’s people (Ps 34:9) or to their priestly leaders (2 Chr 35:3), but here it refers to God’s heavenly assembly and the angels that surround his throne (see vv. 6-7).

verses.zh: 他在圣者的会中，是大有威严的　神，比一切在他四围的更可畏惧。
verses.en: a God who is honored[NOTE:1] in the great angelic assembly,[NOTE:2] and more awesome than[NOTE:3] all who surround him?
notes: Heb “sons of gods”; or “sons of God.” Though אֵלִים (ʾelim) is vocalized as a plural form (“gods”) in the Hebrew text, it is likely that the final mem (ם) is actually enclitic rather than a plural marker. In this case one may read “God.” Some, following a Qumran text and the LXX, also propose the phrase occurred in the original text of Deut 32:8. The phrase בְנֵי אֵלִים (vene ʾelim, “sons of gods” or “sons of God”) occurs only here and in Ps 29:1. Since the “sons of gods/God” are here associated with “the assembly of the holy ones” and “council of the holy ones,” the heavenly assembly (comprised of so-called “angels” and other supernatural beings) appears to be in view. See Job 5:1; 15:15 and Zech 14:5, where these supernatural beings are referred to as “holy ones.” In Canaanite mythological texts the divine council of the high god El is called “the sons of El.” The OT apparently uses the Canaanite phrase, applying it to the supernatural beings that surround the Lord’s heavenly throne.
Heb “feared.”
Heb “in the great assembly of the holy ones.”

verses.zh: 耶和华―万军之　神啊，哪一个大能者像你耶和华？你的信实是在你的四围。
verses.en: O Lord God of Heaven’s Armies![NOTE:1] Who is strong like you, O Lord?Your faithfulness surrounds you.
notes: Or perhaps “feared by.”

verses.zh: 你管辖海的狂傲；波浪翻腾，你就使它平静了。
verses.en: You rule over the proud sea.[NOTE:1] When its waves surge,[NOTE:2] you calm them.
notes: Traditionally “God of hosts.” The title here pictures the Lord as enthroned in the midst of the angelic hosts of heaven.
Heb “the majesty of the sea.”

verses.zh: 你打碎了拉哈伯，似乎是已杀的人；你用有能的膀臂打散了你的仇敌。
verses.en: You crushed the Proud One[NOTE:1] and killed it;[NOTE:2] with your strong arm you scattered your enemies.
notes: Heb “rise up.”

Heb “Rahab.” The name “Rahab” means “proud one.” Since it is sometimes used of Egypt (see Ps 87:4; Isa 30:7), the passage may allude to the exodus. However, the name is also used of the sea (or the mythological sea creature) which symbolizes the disruptive forces of the world that seek to replace order with chaos (see Job 9:13; 26:12). Isa 51:9 appears to combine the mythological and historical referents. The association of Rahab with the sea in Ps 89 (see v. 9) suggests that the name carries symbolic force in this context. In this case the passage may allude to creation (see vv. 11-12), when God overcame the great deep and brought order out of chaos.

verses.zh: 天属你，地也属你；世界和其中所充满的都为你所建立。
verses.en: The heavens belong to you, as does the earth.You made the world and all it contains.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “like one fatally wounded.”

verses.zh: 南北为你所创造；他泊和黑门都因你的名欢呼。
verses.en: You created the north and the south.Tabor and Hermon[NOTE:1] rejoice in your name.
notes: Heb “the world and its fullness, you established them.”

verses.zh: 你有大能的膀臂；你的手有力，你的右手也高举。
verses.en: Your arm is powerful,your hand strong,your right hand[NOTE:1] victorious.[NOTE:2]
notes: Tabor and Hermon were two of the most prominent mountains in Palestine.
The Lord’s arm, hand, and right hand all symbolize his activities, especially his exploits in war.

verses.zh: 公义和公平是你宝座的根基；慈爱和诚实行在你前面。
verses.en: Equity and justice are the foundation of your throne.[NOTE:1] Loyal love and faithfulness characterize your rule.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “is lifted up.” The idiom “the right hand is lifted up” refers to victorious military deeds (see Pss 89:42; 118:16).
The Lord’s throne symbolizes his kingship.

verses.zh: 知道向你欢呼的，那民是有福的！耶和华啊，他们在你脸上的光里行走。
verses.en: How blessed are the people who worship you![NOTE:1] O Lord, they experience your favor.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “are in front of your face.” The idiom can mean “confront” (Ps 17:13) or “meet, enter the presence of” (Ps 95:2).
Heb “who know the shout.” “Shout” here refers to the shouts of the Lord’s worshipers (see Pss 27:6; 33:3; 47:5).

verses.zh: 他们因你的名终日欢乐，因你的公义得以高举。
verses.en: They rejoice in your name all day long,and are vindicated[NOTE:1] by your justice.
notes: Heb “in the light of your face they walk.” The idiom “light of your face” probably refers to a smile (see Eccl 8:1), which in turn suggests favor and blessing (see Num 6:25; Pss 4:6; 31:16; 44:3; 67:1; 80:3, 7, 19; Dan 9:17).

verses.zh: 你是他们力量的荣耀；因为你喜悦我们，我们的角必被高举。
verses.en: For you give them splendor and strength.[NOTE:1] By your favor we are victorious.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “are lifted up.”
Heb “for the splendor of their strength [is] you.”

verses.zh: 我们的盾牌属耶和华；我们的王属以色列的圣者。
verses.en: For our shield[NOTE:1] belongs to the Lord,our king to the Holy One of Israel.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “you lift up our horn,” or if one follows the marginal reading (Qere), “our horn is lifted up.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (see Deut 33:17; 1 Kgs 22:11; Ps 92:10). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see 1 Sam 2:10; Pss 75:10; 89:24; 92:10; Lam 2:17).

The phrase “our shield” refers metaphorically to the Davidic king, who, as God’s vice-regent, was the human protector of the people. Note the parallelism with “our king” here and with “your anointed one” in Ps 84:9.

verses.zh: 当时，你在异象中晓谕你的圣民，说：我已把救助之力加在那有能者的身上；我高举那从民中所拣选的。
verses.en: Then you[NOTE:1] spoke through a vision to your faithful followers[NOTE:2] and said:“I have placed a young hero[NOTE:3] over a warrior;I have raised up a young man[NOTE:4] from the people.
notes: The basic sense of the word “holy” is “set apart from that which is commonplace, special, unique.” The Lord’s holiness is first and foremost his transcendent sovereignty as the ruler of the world. He is “set apart” from the world over which he rules. At the same time his holiness encompasses his moral authority, which derives from his royal position. As king he has the right to dictate to his subjects how they are to live; indeed his very own character sets the standard for proper behavior. This expression is a common title for the Lord in the book of Isaiah.
The pronoun “you” refers to the Lord, who is addressed here. The quotation that follows further develops the announcement of vv. 3-4.
Many medieval mss read the singular here, “your faithful follower.” In this case the statement refers directly to Nathan’s oracle to David (see 2 Sam 7:17).

The MT reads עֵזֶר (ʿezer, “help, strength”), thus “I have placed help on a warrior,” which might effectively mean “I have strengthened a warrior.” The BHS note suggests reading נֵזֶר (nezer, “crown”), similar to the sentiment of anointing in the next verse. HALOT suggests reading עֹזֶר (ʿozer, “hero”) based on an Ugaritic cognate which means “young man, hero, warrior” (HALOT 811 s.v. II עזר). Craigie treats it similarly, taking עזר as “lad/boy/stripling,” parallel to “young man” in the next line, and seeing either David and Saul or David and Goliath as the historical referent (P. C. Craigie, Psalms [WBC], 19:410).

verses.zh: 我寻得我的仆人大卫，用我的圣膏膏他。
verses.en: I have discovered David, my servant.With my holy oil I have anointed him as king.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or perhaps “a chosen one.”

verses.zh: 我的手必使他坚立；我的膀臂也必坚固他。
verses.en: My hand will support him,[NOTE:1] and my arm will strengthen him.
notes: The words “as king” are supplied in the translation for clarification, indicating that a royal anointing is in view.

verses.zh: 仇敌必不勒索他；凶恶之子也不苦害他。
verses.en: No enemy will be able to exact tribute[NOTE:1] from him;[NOTE:2] a violent oppressor will not be able to humiliate him.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “with whom my hand will be firm.”
Heb “an enemy will not exact tribute.” The imperfect is understood in a modal sense, indicating capability or potential.

The translation understands the Hiphil of נָשַׁא (nashaʾ) in the sense of “act as a creditor.” This may allude to the practice of a conqueror forcing his subjects to pay tribute in exchange for “protection.” Another option is to take the verb from a homonymic verbal root meaning “to deceive,” “to trick.” Still another option is to emend the form to יִשָּׂא (yissaʾ), a Qal imperfect from נָאַשׂ (naʾas, “rise up”) and to translate “an enemy will not rise up against him” (see M. Dahood, Psalms [AB], 2:317).

verses.zh: 我要在他面前打碎他的敌人，击杀那恨他的人。
verses.en: I will crush his enemies before him;I will strike down those who hate him.

verses.zh: 只是我的信实和我的慈爱要与他同在；因我的名，他的角必被高举。
verses.en: He will experience my faithfulness and loyal love,[NOTE:1] and by my name he will win victories.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and a son of violence will not oppress him.” The imperfect is understood in a modal sense, indicating capability or potential. The reference to a “son of violence” echoes the language of God’s promise to David in 2 Sam 7:10 (see also 1 Chr 17:9).
Heb “and my faithfulness and my loyal love [will be] with him.”

verses.zh: 我要使他的左手伸到海上，右手伸到河上。
verses.en: I will place his hand over the sea,his right hand over the rivers.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and by my name his horn will be lifted up.” The horn of an ox underlies the metaphor (see Deut 33:17; 1 Kgs 22:11; Ps 92:10). The horn of the wild ox is frequently a metaphor for military strength; the idiom “exalt/lift up the horn” signifies military victory (see 1 Sam 2:10; Pss 75:10; 92:10; Lam 2:17).

verses.zh: 他要称呼我说：你是我的父，是我的　神，是拯救我的磐石。
verses.en: He will call out to me,‘You are my father,[NOTE:1] my God, and the protector who delivers me.’[NOTE:2]
notes: Some identify “the sea” as the Mediterranean and “the rivers” as the Euphrates and its tributaries. However, it is more likely that “the sea” and “the rivers” are symbols for hostile powers that oppose God and the king (see v. 9, as well as Ps 93:3-4).

You are my father. The Davidic king was viewed as God’s “son” (see 2 Sam 7:14; Ps 2:7). The idiom reflects ancient Near Eastern adoption language associated with covenants of grant, by which a lord would reward a faithful subject by elevating him to special status, referred to as “sonship.” Like a son, the faithful subject received an “inheritance,” viewed as an unconditional, eternal gift. Such gifts usually took the form of land and/or an enduring dynasty. See M. Weinfeld, “The Covenant of Grant in the Old Testament and in the Ancient Near East,” JAOS 90 (1970): 184-203, for general discussion and some striking extra-biblical parallels.

verses.zh: 我也要立他为长子，为世上最高的君王。
verses.en: I will appoint him to be my firstborn son,[NOTE:1] the most exalted of the earth’s kings.
notes: Heb “the rocky summit of my deliverance.”

verses.zh: 我要为他存留我的慈爱，直到永远；我与他立的约必要坚定。
verses.en: I will always extend my loyal love to him,and my covenant with him is secure.[NOTE:1]
notes: The firstborn son typically had special status and received special privileges.

verses.zh: 我也要使他的后裔存到永远，使他的宝座如天之久。
verses.en: I will give him an eternal dynasty[NOTE:1] and make his throne as enduring as the skies above.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “forever I will keep for him my loyal love and will make my covenant secure for him.”
Heb “and I will set in place forever his offspring.”

verses.zh: 倘若他的子孙离弃我的律法，不照我的典章行，
verses.en: If his sons reject my lawand disobey my regulations,

verses.zh: 背弃我的律例，不遵守我的诫命，
verses.en: if they break[NOTE:1] my rulesand do not keep my commandments,
notes: Heb “and his throne like the days of the heavens.”

verses.zh: 我就要用杖责罚他们的过犯，用鞭责罚他们的罪孽。
verses.en: I will punish their rebellion by beating them with a club,[NOTE:1] their sin by inflicting them with bruises.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “desecrate.”

Despite the harsh image of beating…with a club, the language reflects a father-son relationship (see v. 30; 2 Sam 7:14). According to Proverbs, a שֵׁבֶט (shevet, “club”) was sometimes utilized to administer corporal punishment to rebellious children (see Prov 13:24; 22:15; 23:13-14; 29:15).tn Heb “I will punish with a club their rebellion.”

verses.zh: 只是我必不将我的慈爱全然收回，也必不叫我的信实废弃。
verses.en: But I will not remove[NOTE:1] my loyal love from himnor be unfaithful to my promise.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “with blows their sin.”

Heb “break”; “make ineffectual.” Some prefer to emend אָפִיר (ʾafir; the Hiphil of פָּרַר, parar, “to break”) to אָסִיר (ʾasir; the Hiphil of סוּר, sur, “to turn aside”), a verb that appears in 2 Sam 7:15.

verses.zh: 我必不背弃我的约，也不改变我口中所出的。
verses.en: I will not break[NOTE:1] my covenantor go back on what I promised.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and I will not deal falsely with my faithfulness.”
Or “desecrate.”

verses.zh: 我一次指着自己的圣洁起誓：我决不向大卫说谎！
verses.en: Once and for all I have vowed by my own holiness,I will never deceive[NOTE:1] David.
notes: Heb “and what proceeds out of my lips I will not alter.”

verses.zh: 他的后裔要存到永远；他的宝座在我面前如日之恒一般，
verses.en: His dynasty will last forever.[NOTE:1] His throne will endure before me, like the sun;[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “lie to.”
Heb “his offspring forever will be.”

verses.zh: 又如月亮永远坚立，如天上确实的见证。（细拉）
verses.en: it will remain stable, like the moon.[NOTE:1] His throne will endure like the skies.”[NOTE:2] (Selah)
notes: Heb “and his throne like the sun before me.”
Heb “like the moon it will be established forever.”

verses.zh: 但你恼怒你的受膏者，就丢掉弃绝他。
verses.en: But you have spurned[NOTE:1] and rejected him;you are angry with your chosen king.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and a witness in the sky, secure.” Scholars have offered a variety of opinions as to the identity of the “witness” referred to here, none of which is very convincing. It is preferable to join וְעֵד (veʿed) to עוֹלָם (ʿolam) in the preceding line and translate the commonly attested phrase עוֹלָם וְעֵד (“forever”). In this case one may translate the second line, “[it] will be secure like the skies.” Another option (the one reflected in the present translation) is to take עד as a rare noun meaning “throne” or “dais.” This noun is attested in Ugaritic; see, for example, CTA 16 vi 22-23, where ksi (= כִּסֵּא, kisseʾ, “throne”) and ʿd (= עד, “dais”) appear as synonyms in the poetic parallelism (see G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 91). Emending בַּשַּׁחַק (bashakhaq, “in the heavens”) to כַּשַׁחַק (kashakhaq, “like the heavens”)—bet/kaf (כ/ב) confusion is widely attested—one can then read “[his] throne like the heavens [is] firm/stable.” Verse 29 refers to the enduring nature of the heavens, while Job 37:18 speaks of God spreading out the heavens (שְׁחָקִים, shekhaqim) and compares their strength to a bronze mirror. Ps 89:29 uses the term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim, “skies”) which frequently appears in parallelism to שְׁחָקִים.
The Hebrew construction (conjunction + pronoun, followed by the verb) draws attention to the contrast between what follows and what precedes.

verses.zh: 你厌恶了与仆人所立的约，将他的冠冕践踏于地。
verses.en: You have repudiated[NOTE:1] your covenant with your servant;[NOTE:2] you have thrown his crown to the ground.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “your anointed one.” The Hebrew phrase מְשִׁיחֶךָ (meshikhekha, “your anointed one”) refers here to the Davidic king (see Pss 2:2; 18:50; 20:6; 28:8; 84:9; 132:10, 17).
The Hebrew verb appears only here and in Lam 2:7.
Heb “the covenant of your servant.”

verses.zh: 你拆毁了他一切的篱笆，使他的保障变为荒场。
verses.en: You have broken down all his[NOTE:1] walls;you have made his strongholds a heap of ruins.
notes: Heb “you dishonor [or “desecrate”] on the ground his crown.”

verses.zh: 凡过路的人都抢夺他；他成为邻邦的羞辱。
verses.en: All who pass by[NOTE:1] have robbed him;he has become an object of disdain to his neighbors.
notes: The king here represents the land and cities over which he rules.

verses.zh: 你高举了他敌人的右手；你叫他一切的仇敌欢喜。
verses.en: You have allowed his adversaries to be victorious[NOTE:1] and all his enemies to rejoice.
notes: Heb “all the passersby on the road.”

verses.zh: 你叫他的刀剑卷刃，叫他在争战之中站立不住。
verses.en: You turn back[NOTE:1] his sword from the adversary[NOTE:2] and have not sustained him in battle.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “you have lifted up the right hand of his adversaries.” The idiom “the right hand is lifted up” refers to victorious military deeds (see Pss 89:13; 118:16).

The perfect verbal form predominates in vv. 38-45. The use of the imperfect in this one instance may be for rhetorical effect. The psalmist briefly lapses into dramatic mode, describing the king’s military defeat as if it were happening before his very eyes.

Heb “you turn back, rocky summit, his sword.” The Hebrew term צוּר (tsur, “rocky summit”) makes no sense here, unless it is a divine title understood as vocative, “you turn back, O Rocky Summit, his sword.” Some emend the form to צֹר (tsor, “flint”) on the basis of Josh 5:2, which uses the phrase חַרְבוֹת צֻרִים (kharvot tsurim, “flint knives”). The noun צֹר (tsor, “flint”) can then be taken as “flint-like edge,” indicating the sharpness of the sword. Others emend the form to אָחוֹר (ʾakhor, “backward”) or to מִצַּר (mitsar, “from the adversary”). The present translation reflects the latter, assuming an original reading תָּשִׁיב מִצָּר חַרְבּוֹ (tashiv mitsar kharbo), which was changed to תָּשִׁיב צָר חַרְבּוֹ (tashiv tsar kharbo) by virtual haplography (confusion of bet/mem is well-attested) with צָר (tsar, “adversary”) then being misinterpreted as צוּר in the later tradition.

verses.zh: 你使他的光辉止息，将他的宝座推倒于地。
verses.en: You have brought to an end his splendor[NOTE:1] and have knocked[NOTE:2] his throne to the ground.
notes: Heb “and you have not caused him to stand in the battle.”

Rather than the MT’s מִטְּהָרוֹ (mitteharo, “from his splendor”), the text should be read without the dagesh as מִטְהָרוֹ (mitharo, “his splendor”) or possibly as מַטֵּה טְהָרוֹ (matteh teharo, “the staff of his splendor”).

verses.zh: 你减少他青年的日子，又使他蒙羞。（细拉）
verses.en: You have cut short his youth[NOTE:1] and have covered him with shame. (Selah)
notes: The Hebrew verb מָגַר (magar) occurs only here and perhaps in Ezek 21:17.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，这要到几时呢？你要将自己隐藏到永远吗？你的忿怒如火焚烧要到几时呢？
verses.en: How long, O Lord, will this last?Will you remain hidden forever?[NOTE:1] Will your anger continue to burn like fire?
notes: Heb “the days of his youth” (see as well Job 33:25).

verses.zh: 求你想念我的时候是何等的短少；你创造世人，要使他们归何等的虚空呢？
verses.en: Take note of my brief lifespan.[NOTE:1] Why do you make all people so mortal?[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “How long, O Lord, will hide yourself forever?”

Heb “remember me, what is [my] lifespan.” The Hebrew term חֶלֶד (kheled) is also used of one’s lifespan in Ps 39:5. Because the Hebrew text is so awkward here, some prefer to emend it to read מֶה חָדֵל אָנִי (meh khadel ʾani, “[remember] how transient [that is, “short-lived”] I am”; see Ps 39:4).

verses.zh: 谁能常活免死、救他的灵魂脱离阴间的权柄呢？（细拉）
verses.en: No man can live on without experiencing deathor deliver his life from the power of Sheol.[NOTE:1] (Selah)
notes: Heb “For what emptiness do you create all the sons of mankind?” In this context the term שָׁוְא (shavʾ) refers to mankind’s mortal nature and the brevity of life (see vv. 45, 48).

verses.zh: 主啊，你从前凭你的信实向大卫立誓要施行的慈爱在哪里呢？
verses.en: Where are your earlier faithful deeds,[NOTE:1] O Lord,[NOTE:2] the ones performed in accordance with your reliable oath to David?[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Who [is] the man [who] can live and not see death, [who] can deliver his life from the hand of Sheol?” The rhetorical question anticipates the answer, “No one!”
The Lord’s faithful deeds are also mentioned in Pss 17:7 and 25:6.
Many medieval Hebrew mss read here יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”).

verses.zh: 主啊，求你记念仆人们所受的羞辱，记念我怎样将一切强盛民的羞辱存在我怀里。
verses.en: Take note, O Lord,[NOTE:1] of the way your servants are taunted[NOTE:2] and of how I must bear so many insults from people.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “[which] you swore on oath to David by your faithfulness.”
Many medieval Hebrew mss read here יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”).
Heb “remember, O Lord, the taunt against your servants.” Many medieval Hebrew mss read the singular here, “your servant” (that is, the psalmist).

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你的仇敌用这羞辱羞辱了你的仆人，羞辱了你受膏者的脚踪。
verses.en: Your enemies, O Lord, hurl insults;they insult your chosen king as they dog his footsteps.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “my lifting up in my arms [or “against my chest”] all of the many, peoples.” The term רַבִּים (rabbim, “many”) makes no apparent sense here. For this reason some emend the text to רִבֵי (rive, “attacks by”), a defectively written plural construct form of רִיב (riv, “dispute; quarrel”).

verses.zh: 耶和华是应当称颂的，直到永远。阿们！阿们！
verses.en: [NOTE:1] The Lord deserves praise[NOTE:2] forevermore!We agree! We agree![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “[by] which your enemies, O Lord, taunt, [by] which they taunt [at] the heels of your anointed one.”

The final verse of Ps 89, v. 52, is a conclusion to this third “book” (or major editorial division) of the Psalter. Similar statements appear at or near the end of each of the first, second and fourth “books” of the Psalter (see Pss 41:13; 72:18-19; 106:48, respectively).
Heb “[be] blessed.” See Pss 18:46; 28:6; 31:21.
